questions.q: Organophosphates such as malathion, parathion, and the nerve agent sarin produce toxicity by which mechanism?
ch: Excess release of norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve terminals
Competitive antagonism of nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction
Phosphorylation and inhibition of acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at synapses
Blockade of muscarinic receptors, preventing acetylcholine from reaching its target
Depletion of acetylcholine from presynaptic vesicles, leaving synapses empty
questions.exp: Organophosphates phosphorylate and inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS synapses — the tri-receptor basis of cholinergic crisis.
why: The toxidrome is cholinergic; it is not driven by catecholamine release.
Nicotinic receptors are overstimulated by the excess acetylcholine, producing fasciculations and weakness, not competitively blocked.
Muscarinic blockade is how atropine treats the poisoning, not how the poison works.
Acetylcholine floods the synapse in this poisoning; it is not depleted.

questions.q: Which cluster of findings represents the muscarinic (SLUDGE/DUMBELS) component of organophosphate toxicity?
ch: Hypertension, tachycardia, and laryngospasm during a rapid intravenous push
Salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramping, and emesis
Muscle fasciculations, weakness, tachycardia, and mydriasis
Agitation, seizures, and coma without any peripheral findings
Dry mouth, flushed skin, hyperthermia, and urinary retention
questions.exp: SLUDGE — Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI cramping, Emesis — is the muscarinic cholinergic toxidrome; the DUMBELS version adds miosis and bradycardia.
why: Those effects follow a too-rapid intravenous pralidoxime push, not muscarinic stimulation.
These are the nicotinic effects, which conflict with the muscarinic signs and create the classic opposing-sign pitfall.
Agitation, seizures, and coma are the CNS component of the tri-receptor toxidrome, not the muscarinic one.
Dry skin, hyperthermia, and urinary retention describe anticholinergic toxicity from over-atropinization — the opposite of cholinergic excess.

questions.q: The "Killer B's" name the features that actually cause death in organophosphate poisoning. Which triad is it?
ch: Blindness, bulbar weakness, and blistering of exposed skin
Bradycardia, bruising, and bacteremia from secondary infection
Bradypnea, bradykinesia, and bilateral miosis
Bradycardia, bronchorrhea, and bronchospasm
Bronchiectasis, bleeding, and bilateral fasciculations
questions.exp: The Killer B's are bradycardia, bronchorrhea, and bronchospasm: respiratory failure from copious secretions and bronchospasm, compounded by diaphragmatic weakness, is the leading cause of death.
why: Blistering and blindness are not features of the cholinergic toxidrome; miosis, not blindness, is the ocular finding.
Bradycardia belongs, but bruising and bacteremia are not part of this toxidrome.
Miosis is a real muscarinic sign but bradykinesia is not, and the lethal problem is secretions and bronchospasm.
Fasciculations are nicotinic and real, but bronchiectasis and bleeding are not features of acute poisoning.

questions.q: Atropine is being titrated in a patient with organophosphate poisoning. What is the correct therapeutic endpoint?
ch: Drying of pulmonary secretions with clear breath sounds and adequate oxygenation
Complete resolution of muscle fasciculations and proximal weakness
Normalization of the red-blood-cell acetylcholinesterase level
A heart rate consistently above 100 beats per minute
Dilation of the pinpoint pupils back to a normal size
questions.exp: Atropine is titrated to drying of pulmonary secretions — clear lungs and adequate oxygenation — explicitly not to heart rate or pupil size; doubling the dose every few minutes is standard and large cumulative amounts may be required.
why: Fasciculations and weakness are nicotinic and do not respond to atropine — that is what pralidoxime is for.
Cholinesterase levels are confirmatory tests that treatment must not wait on, let alone be titrated to.
Heart rate is explicitly not the endpoint, and it is unreliable here because nicotinic and muscarinic effects push it in opposite directions.
Pupil size is explicitly not the endpoint; miosis may persist after the lungs are dry.

questions.q: Why is pralidoxime (2-PAM) added to atropine rather than giving atropine alone?
ch: It sedates the patient and terminates cholinergic seizures more reliably
It blocks muscarinic receptors more completely than atropine and dries secretions faster
It is withheld until enzyme aging is complete and then restores the phosphorylated enzyme
It chelates the organophosphate in the bloodstream so the kidneys can clear it
It reactivates acetylcholinesterase and reverses nicotinic fasciculations and weakness that atropine cannot
questions.exp: Pralidoxime is an oxime that reactivates acetylcholinesterase, addressing the nicotinic fasciculations and weakness atropine cannot touch; it must be given early, before the enzyme-phosphate bond ages, and always alongside atropine.
why: Benzodiazepines, not the oxime, are first-line for organophosphate-induced seizures and agitation.
Muscarinic blockade is atropine's job; the oxime works on the enzyme itself.
This inverts the timing — once the bond ages, pralidoxime is ineffective, so it must be given early.
Pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme rather than binding and clearing the poison.

questions.q: A patient with organophosphate poisoning needs intubation for respiratory failure. Which agent should be avoided, and why?
ch: Midazolam — benzodiazepines are contraindicated in cholinergic poisoning
Pralidoxime — the oxime must be held until the airway has been secured
Supplemental oxygen — a high inspired fraction aggravates cholinergic seizures
Succinylcholine — cholinesterase inhibition markedly prolongs its paralysis
Atropine — it worsens bronchorrhea and must be stopped before airway management
questions.exp: Succinylcholine must never be used: its paralysis is dangerously prolonged by cholinesterase inhibition. Aggressive atropinization to reduce secretions is prioritized before intubation when feasible.
why: Benzodiazepines are first-line for organophosphate-induced seizures and agitation.
Pralidoxime should be given early, before enzyme aging, not deferred for the airway.
Oxygen is part of treatment for hypoxia from bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, and diaphragmatic weakness.
Atropine dries secretions and is the first-line antidote; it is escalated, not stopped, around intubation.

questions.q: An organophosphate-poisoned patient begins seizing. Which treatment is first-line?
ch: Succinylcholine to abolish the motor activity while ventilating
Phenytoin, the preferred anticonvulsant for this toxidrome
Escalating atropine alone until the seizure activity stops
A rapid intravenous push of pralidoxime to reactivate the enzyme
A benzodiazepine such as diazepam, midazolam, or lorazepam
questions.exp: Benzodiazepines — diazepam, midazolam, or lorazepam — are first-line for organophosphate-induced seizures and agitation, and are given prophylactically in severe nerve-agent exposure; monitor for respiratory depression and support the airway.
why: Succinylcholine must be avoided entirely here, and paralysis would mask rather than treat the seizure.
Phenytoin is ineffective for organophosphate-induced seizures.
Atropine reverses muscarinic effects and is titrated to dry lungs; it is not the anticonvulsant.
A too-rapid pralidoxime push causes hypertension, tachycardia, and laryngospasm, and the oxime is not an anticonvulsant.

questions.q: A farmer treated for organophosphate poisoning improved and was weaned off atropine. On hospital day 3 he develops proximal limb weakness and a falling tidal volume. What is happening?
ch: Organophosphate-induced delayed polyneuropathy, which appears weeks after exposure
The intermediate syndrome — proximal and respiratory muscle weakness 24-96 hours after exposure
Anticholinergic toxicity from over-atropinization, with hyperthermia and delirium
Carbamate poisoning, whose cholinesterase inhibition is reversible and transient
Laryngospasm caused by a too-rapid pralidoxime infusion
questions.exp: New proximal and respiratory muscle weakness 24-96 hours after apparent recovery is the intermediate syndrome, a red flag demanding urgent ventilatory support — which is why monitoring continues even in the improving patient.
why: OPIDN is the third temporal syndrome but it appears weeks later, not on day 3.
Over-atropinization causes hyperthermia, delirium, and urinary retention rather than proximal and respiratory weakness, and the atropine had already been weaned.
Carbamate inhibition is transient and reversible; it does not produce a delayed weakness syndrome.
Infusion-related laryngospasm is immediate and upper-airway, not a day-3 proximal muscle weakness.

questions.q: Which laboratory test best confirms organophosphate exposure, and how should it affect management?
ch: Arterial blood gas, which establishes the diagnosis of cholinergic crisis
The QTc interval on the ECG, which confirms cholinesterase inhibition
Red-blood-cell acetylcholinesterase, which best reflects the synaptic effect — but treatment must not wait for it
Plasma (butyryl) cholinesterase, the more specific of the two available assays
A quantitative serum organophosphate concentration drawn before atropine
questions.exp: Red-blood-cell acetylcholinesterase is the confirmatory test that best reflects the synaptic effect, yet the diagnosis is made clinically from the toxidrome and history — empiric atropine and pralidoxime cannot wait on the result.
why: An ABG is an adjunct that measures respiratory failure; it does not confirm the exposure.
QTc prolongation and bradyarrhythmias are monitored on the ECG but they do not confirm the diagnosis.
Plasma cholinesterase is also sent, but the red-blood-cell enzyme better reflects the synaptic effect.
Management rests on the toxidrome and cholinesterase activity, not on a quantitative poison level.

questions.q: Two farm workers arrive in wet, pesticide-soaked clothing with pinpoint pupils and a garlic odor. Which action protects both the patients and the staff before hands-on care begins?
ch: Don chemical-protective equipment, then remove and bag the clothing and irrigate the skin
Begin hands-on care at once, since dermal absorption stops once a patient is indoors
Paralyze and intubate both patients with succinylcholine before decontamination
Send red-blood-cell acetylcholinesterase and await the result before any treatment
Give activated charcoal to both patients regardless of the route of exposure
questions.exp: Decontamination stops ongoing dermal absorption and protects staff: rescuers don chemical-protective equipment, contaminated clothing is removed and bagged, and the skin and eyes are copiously irrigated. Signs of staff or bystander contamination mean PPE and decontamination have failed.
why: Absorption continues from contaminated skin and clothing, and unprotected hands-on care causes secondary contamination of staff.
Succinylcholine is contraindicated because cholinesterase inhibition prolongs its paralysis, and decontamination cannot be skipped.
Treatment is empiric and must never wait on the confirmatory cholinesterase result.
Charcoal may be considered for recent large ingestions per poison-control guidance, not for a dermal exposure.

questions.q: Which histologic type accounts for most breast cancers?
ch: Invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type), roughly 70-80% of cases
Squamous cell carcinoma arising from the overlying skin of the nipple
Sarcoma arising from the fibrous stroma between the lobules
Invasive lobular carcinoma, the commonest invasive subtype by a wide margin
Lobular carcinoma in situ, a true precursor that has breached the basement membrane
questions.exp: Invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC, no special type) arises from the terminal duct-lobular unit and accounts for roughly 70-80% of cases, making it the most common type.
why: Breast cancers are adenocarcinomas of glandular origin, not squamous skin cancers.
Stromal sarcomas of the breast are rare; the overwhelming majority are adenocarcinomas.
Invasive lobular carcinoma is the second most common invasive type, not the first.
LCIS is a risk marker rather than a true precursor, and in-situ disease by definition has not breached the basement membrane.

questions.q: How do ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) differ?
ch: Both have breached the basement membrane and are therefore staged as invasive
DCIS is defined by HER2 amplification and LCIS by estrogen-receptor positivity
Neither lesion is visible on mammography, so both are found only at mastectomy
DCIS is a non-invasive lesion that has not breached the basement membrane, while LCIS is a risk marker rather than a true precursor
DCIS is only a risk marker, while LCIS is the true precursor of invasive cancer
questions.exp: DCIS is the non-invasive lesion that has not breached the basement membrane; LCIS, by contrast, is regarded as a risk marker rather than a true precursor lesion.
why: In-situ disease by definition has not breached the basement membrane.
Receptor status is tested on the tumor to guide therapy; it does not define these in-situ lesions.
In-situ lesions are frequently screen-detected, and mastectomy is not required to identify them.
This reverses the two — LCIS is the risk marker and DCIS the non-invasive lesion.

questions.q: A biopsy is reported as ER-negative, PR-negative, and HER2-negative. What does that mean for treatment?
ch: It is endocrine-responsive, so a CDK4/6 inhibitor plus endocrine therapy is standard
It is triple-negative disease, with no targeted receptor therapy and a worse prognosis
It is hormone-driven and should be treated with tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor
It is HER2-amplified and should receive trastuzumab with pertuzumab and chemotherapy
It cannot be treated with any systemic therapy and is managed with surgery alone
questions.exp: ER-negative, PR-negative, HER2-negative disease is triple-negative: there is no targeted receptor to exploit and the prognosis is worse, so a cytotoxic chemotherapy backbone of an anthracycline plus a taxane carries the treatment.
why: CDK4/6 inhibitors are added to endocrine therapy in hormone-receptor-positive disease, not in triple-negative disease.
Endocrine therapy requires ER positivity; it has nothing to act on in an ER-negative tumor.
Anti-HER2 therapy is for HER2-positive disease; this tumor is HER2-negative.
Cytotoxic chemotherapy is very much used in triple-negative disease, and PARP inhibitors are an option in BRCA-mutated tumors.

questions.q: Which screening strategy does the module cite for breast cancer?
ch: Mammography as the primary tool, with USPSTF biennial screening from ages 40 to 74
No screening until a palpable mass appears, then a diagnostic mammogram
Annual mammography starting at age 25 for all women regardless of their risk
Clinical breast examination alone until age 50, then mammography every five years
Breast MRI as the primary screening tool for women at average risk
questions.exp: Screening mammography is the primary tool, and the USPSTF now recommends biennial screening from ages 40 to 74; high-risk women (BRCA carriers, prior chest radiation) add annual breast MRI.
why: Waiting for a palpable mass defeats the purpose of screening, which is to find disease before it is felt.
Average-risk screening starts around age 40, not 25, and intensity is risk-stratified.
Examination does not substitute for mammography, and a five-year interval is far too long.
MRI is added annually for high-risk women such as BRCA carriers; it is not the average-risk tool.

questions.q: Why is core needle biopsy, rather than fine-needle aspiration, required to diagnose breast cancer?
ch: Because it removes the entire lesion and therefore serves as definitive treatment
Because it establishes the TNM stage without any need for further imaging
Because it is the only breast biopsy that can be performed under ultrasound guidance
Because FNA cannot reach lesions that were detected only on screening mammography
Because it preserves architecture for histologic grade and for ER, PR, and HER2 testing
questions.exp: Definitive diagnosis requires core needle biopsy because it preserves architecture for histologic grade plus receptor testing — ER and PR by IHC, HER2 by IHC or FISH — which FNA cannot reliably provide.
why: A core biopsy samples the lesion; surgery (lumpectomy or mastectomy) is the definitive local treatment.
Staging integrates tumor size, nodes, and metastasis and often needs imaging; biopsy alone does not supply it.
Both core biopsy and FNA can be ultrasound-guided; guidance is not what distinguishes them.
Image-guided sampling can reach non-palpable lesions; the issue is the quality of the tissue obtained.

questions.q: A premenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer is starting tamoxifen. Which counseling point is most important?
ch: Monitor complete blood counts for neutropenia and obtain an ECG before each cycle
The drug is a vesicant, so the infusion site must be watched for extravasation
Report abnormal vaginal bleeding or leg swelling, given the endometrial cancer and VTE risk
Expect arthralgias and accelerated bone loss, so bone density will be monitored
Serial echocardiograms are required because the drug lowers ejection fraction
questions.exp: Tamoxifen is a SERM that is anti-estrogenic in the breast but pro-estrogenic on the uterus, so it increases the risk of endometrial cancer and venous thromboembolism — abnormal vaginal bleeding or leg swelling must be reported.
why: Neutropenia monitoring and ECG surveillance for QT prolongation belong to the CDK4/6 inhibitors.
Extravasation precautions apply to intravenous vesicants such as doxorubicin, not to an oral endocrine agent.
Arthralgias and bone loss are the aromatase-inhibitor profile, and AIs are not used alone in premenopausal women.
A falling LVEF is the trastuzumab and anthracycline concern, not a tamoxifen effect.

questions.q: Which monitoring is required before and during trastuzumab therapy for HER2-positive breast cancer?
ch: Serial complete blood counts, since neutropenia is the dose-limiting toxicity
Baseline and serial echocardiography or MUGA for a decline in ejection fraction
Baseline and serial bone density scans to detect accelerated bone loss
Serial endometrial biopsies because of the risk of uterine malignancy
Baseline and periodic nerve conduction studies for sensory neuropathy
questions.exp: Trastuzumab causes cardiotoxicity with a decreased LVEF, so a baseline and serial echocardiogram or MUGA are obtained and concurrent anthracycline overlap is avoided.
why: Neutropenia monitoring belongs to cytotoxic chemotherapy and the CDK4/6 inhibitors.
Bone density monitoring belongs to the aromatase inhibitors, which accelerate bone loss.
Endometrial cancer risk is a tamoxifen effect; abnormal bleeding prompts evaluation.
Neuropathy is a taxane toxicity and is followed clinically, not by routine conduction studies.

questions.q: A woman has a rapidly enlarging, erythematous, warm, edematous breast with peau d'orange. What is the concern?
ch: Ductal carcinoma in situ, which is confined and carries an excellent prognosis
Lymphedema of the breast following prior axillary surgery on that side
Acute mastitis, which should be treated with oral antibiotics and warm compresses
A benign fibrocystic change that fluctuates with the menstrual cycle
Inflammatory breast cancer, aggressive clinical stage III/IV disease, not an infection
questions.exp: Rapid-onset erythema with peau d'orange indicates inflammatory breast cancer — aggressive disease that is clinical stage III/IV rather than an infection, and it must not be dismissed as mastitis.
why: DCIS is non-invasive and does not cause an inflamed, edematous breast.
Post-surgical lymphedema follows axillary intervention and does not present as a new rapidly enlarging erythematous breast.
Treating this as an infection is the classic error; the module warns explicitly not to dismiss it as mastitis.
Fibrocystic change does not produce rapidly progressive erythema, warmth, and skin edema.

questions.q: A patient has just undergone axillary lymph node dissection. Which nursing measure protects the affected arm?
ch: Draw all laboratory samples from that arm in order to spare the unoperated side
Delay reporting any arm swelling until the surgical drains have been removed
Immobilize the arm in a sling and avoid all movement of it for six weeks
Use no blood pressure cuffs, venipunctures, or IVs on that side, and teach lymphedema prevention
Apply ice to the axilla continuously and restrict the patient's oral fluid intake
questions.exp: After axillary surgery or node dissection the affected arm is protected — no blood pressure cuffs, venipunctures, or IVs on that side — and the patient is taught lymphedema prevention and early reporting of arm swelling.
why: This is exactly backwards — venipunctures on the operated side raise the lymphedema and infection risk.
Arm swelling should be reported early, because early recognition is central to lymphedema management.
Prolonged immobilization is not the teaching; protecting the arm from cuffs and needles while restoring function is.
Neither continuous ice nor fluid restriction is part of lymphedema prevention.

questions.q: A 58-year-old woman has a node-negative, ER-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer. Which tool helps decide whether she benefits from chemotherapy?
ch: A bone scan and PET to search for occult metastatic disease
BI-RADS scoring of the diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound
A genomic assay such as the Oncotype DX recurrence score
Sentinel lymph node biopsy performed after completion of surgery
HER2 testing by FISH, repeated on the surgical specimen
questions.exp: Genomic assays such as the Oncotype DX recurrence score help decide chemotherapy benefit in early-stage ER-positive, HER2-negative, node-negative breast cancer.
why: Metastatic imaging is reserved for advanced disease workup, not for an early node-negative tumor.
BI-RADS grades imaging findings to guide biopsy; it says nothing about chemotherapy benefit.
Sentinel node biopsy evaluates the axilla at the time of surgery, and this axilla is already node-negative.
HER2 status is already known to be negative here; repeating it does not answer the chemotherapy question.

questions.q: Which sequence describes how most colorectal cancers develop?
ch: Direct spread of a gastric adenocarcinoma along the wall of the transverse colon
Chronic mucosal ischemia progressing directly to an invasive squamous carcinoma
Hyperplasia of neuroendocrine cells progressing to a carcinoid tumor of the colon
Malignant transformation of a submucosal lipoma into an invasive adenocarcinoma
Normal mucosa to adenomatous polyp to invasive cancer, driven by APC, KRAS, and TP53
questions.exp: Over 95% of colorectal cancers are adenocarcinomas arising through the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence — normal mucosa to adenomatous polyp to invasive cancer — as APC is lost and KRAS and TP53 mutations accumulate, which is why polypectomy is preventive.
why: These are primary colorectal tumors arising from their own mucosa, not gastric extension.
Colorectal cancers are adenocarcinomas of glandular mucosa, and ischemia is not the driver.
Carcinoid tumors are a separate and far less common entity than adenocarcinoma.
A lipoma is benign mesenchymal tissue and is not the precursor lesion; the adenomatous polyp is.

questions.q: Which test is the gold standard for confirming colorectal cancer?
ch: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with intravenous contrast
Colonoscopy with biopsy, which also removes synchronous polyps
Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) drawn at the time of presentation
Barium enema demonstrating a napkin-ring filling defect
Endorectal ultrasound of the distal rectum and perirectal tissue
questions.exp: Colonoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard: it visualizes and biopsies the lesion and removes synchronous polyps at the same sitting.
why: CT is for metastatic staging of the liver and lungs; it provides no tissue diagnosis.
CEA is a baseline prognostic and surveillance marker, not a diagnostic or screening test.
Barium enema is largely historical and may suggest an apple-core lesion, but it cannot biopsy it.
Endorectal ultrasound assesses local T-stage in rectal cancer rather than establishing the diagnosis.

questions.q: At what age should colorectal cancer screening begin in average-risk adults, and at what colonoscopy interval?
ch: Age 45, with colonoscopy every 10 years
Age 30, with colonoscopy every 3 years
Age 40, with colonoscopy every 5 years
Age 50, with colonoscopy every 15 years
Age 60, with a single lifetime colonoscopy
questions.exp: Screening begins at age 45 for average-risk adults, and colonoscopy every 10 years is the gold-standard modality; polypectomy at screening interrupts the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
why: Age 30 is earlier than the average-risk threshold; that intensity is reserved for hereditary syndromes.
Average-risk screening starts at 45, and the standard colonoscopy interval is 10 years.
The threshold was lowered from 50 to 45, and no guideline supports a 15-year interval.
Starting at 60 misses a decade and a half of preventable disease, and screening is repeated rather than one-time.

questions.q: How do right-sided and left-sided colorectal tumors typically differ in presentation?
ch: Left-sided tumors metastasize only to bone, while right-sided tumors spare the liver
Right-sided tumors bleed occultly and cause iron-deficiency anemia; left-sided tumors constrict and obstruct
Right-sided tumors obstruct early, while left-sided tumors present with iron-deficiency anemia
Both sides present identically, with painless rectal bleeding and no anemia at all
Right-sided tumors cause pencil-thin stools, while left-sided tumors stay bulky and silent
questions.exp: Right-sided (proximal) tumors are bulky and bleed occultly, producing iron-deficiency anemia, while left-sided (distal) tumors are annular and constricting, producing obstruction and a change in stool caliber — right bleeds, left obstructs.
why: Liver and lung are the common metastatic sites for colorectal cancer regardless of side.
This reverses the mnemonic: right bleeds, left obstructs.
Side-specific presentation is a reliable localization clue, and occult bleeding commonly does cause anemia.
Pencil-thin stools reflect a constricting left-sided lesion; the bulky lesions are right-sided.

questions.q: What is the correct use of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) in colorectal cancer?
ch: It replaces surveillance colonoscopy once the primary tumor has been resected
It is the screening test of choice for average-risk adults from age 45 onward
It establishes the diagnosis whenever it is above the laboratory reference range
It is a prognostic and surveillance marker — a rising post-operative level suggests recurrence
It determines whether anti-EGFR therapy may be used in metastatic disease
questions.exp: CEA is drawn as a baseline and trended as a prognostic and surveillance marker, because a persistently elevated or rising post-operative level suggests residual or recurrent disease.
why: Serial CEA and surveillance colonoscopy are complementary; neither replaces the other.
CEA is explicitly not a screening test; colonoscopy is the screening modality from age 45.
Diagnosis requires colonoscopy with biopsy; an elevated marker alone proves nothing.
RAS mutational status, not CEA, decides eligibility for cetuximab or panitumumab.

questions.q: A CT colonography report describes a circumferential constricting annular filling defect. What is this classically called, and what does it signify?
ch: A right-sided bulky mass that bleeds occultly without ever obstructing
A napkin-ring stricture caused by Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum
An apple-core lesion, signalling an obstructing colorectal adenocarcinoma, typically left-sided
A lead-pipe colon produced by long-standing ulcerative colitis
A pedunculated adenomatous polyp that is still confined to the mucosa
questions.exp: The apple-core (napkin-ring) lesion is a circumferential constricting annular filling defect that signals an obstructing colorectal adenocarcinoma, classically on the left side.
why: Bulky occultly bleeding lesions are the right-sided pattern; this description is of a constricting tumor.
The napkin-ring name refers to this malignant annular lesion, and the description here is of a constricting colonic cancer.
Lead-pipe colon is a diffuse featureless colon, not a focal annular constricting defect.
A polyp projects into the lumen; it does not constrict the bowel circumferentially.

questions.q: A patient starting FOLFOX asks what to expect. Which teaching point is specific to oxaliplatin?
ch: Avoid cold drinks and cold exposure, which trigger a peripheral sensory neuropathy
Expect a cholinergic diarrhea within minutes of the infusion starting
Take the oral tablets twice daily and watch for hand-foot syndrome
Report an acneiform rash, which correlates with response to the drug
Expect mucositis and diarrhea, and be screened for DPD deficiency first
questions.exp: Oxaliplatin's signature toxicity is a cold-induced peripheral sensory neuropathy, so patients are taught to avoid cold drinks and cold exposure; the neuropathy is cumulative and dose-limiting.
why: Early cholinergic diarrhea is an irinotecan effect, seen in FOLFIRI rather than FOLFOX.
Hand-foot syndrome with an oral 5-FU prodrug describes capecitabine; oxaliplatin is given intravenously.
The acneiform rash that correlates with response belongs to the anti-EGFR antibodies cetuximab and panitumumab.
Mucositis, diarrhea, and DPD-deficiency screening belong to 5-FU and leucovorin, the other half of FOLFOX.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man is found to have iron-deficiency anemia on routine labs with no overt bleeding. What is the next step?
ch: Start oral iron replacement and recheck the hemoglobin in three months
Order a CEA level to determine whether an occult malignancy is present
Obtain a barium enema, looking for the classic apple-core filling defect
Reassure him, since iron-deficiency anemia in adult men is usually dietary
Perform colonoscopy with biopsy — this anemia is colon cancer until proven otherwise
questions.exp: Iron-deficiency anemia in an older man or a postmenopausal woman is colon cancer until proven otherwise, because right-sided lesions bleed occultly — colonoscopy with biopsy is mandated.
why: Replacing iron without finding the source of the blood loss delays a cancer diagnosis.
CEA is a prognostic and surveillance marker and cannot be used to rule a malignancy in or out.
Barium enema is largely historical and cannot biopsy; colonoscopy both visualizes and samples.
Iron-deficiency anemia in an older man is precisely the presentation that mandates colonoscopy.

questions.q: A resected colon cancer is node-positive (stage III) with no distant metastases. What is the standard adjuvant therapy?
ch: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation, delivered after the resection
Surveillance CEA and colonoscopy with no chemotherapy at all
FOLFOX — 5-FU with leucovorin plus oxaliplatin
Cetuximab alone, regardless of the tumor's RAS status
Pembrolizumab alone, regardless of the tumor's MSI/MMR status
questions.exp: Adjuvant FOLFOX — 5-FU and leucovorin plus oxaliplatin — is standard for node-positive stage III colon cancer; resection alone suffices only for earlier localized disease.
why: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation precedes surgery and is for locally advanced rectal cancer, not resected colon cancer.
Surveillance is part of follow-up, but node-positive disease warrants adjuvant chemotherapy.
Anti-EGFR antibodies are used in metastatic disease and only when the tumor is RAS wild-type.
Pembrolizumab is reserved for MSI-high or mismatch-repair-deficient metastatic tumors.

questions.q: Before starting cetuximab or panitumumab in metastatic colorectal cancer, which result must be confirmed?
ch: A UGT1A1 polymorphism placing the patient at low risk
MSI-high or mismatch-repair-deficient tumor status
A BRAF V600E mutation in the primary tumor
RAS wild-type status — KRAS and NRAS not mutated
A normal serum magnesium at the time of the first dose
questions.exp: Anti-EGFR antibodies are used in metastatic disease only if the tumor is RAS wild-type, meaning KRAS and NRAS are not mutated; they are ineffective and potentially harmful in RAS-mutant tumors.
why: UGT1A1 polymorphisms modify irinotecan toxicity risk, not anti-EGFR eligibility.
MSI-high/dMMR status selects patients for pembrolizumab immunotherapy and triggers a Lynch syndrome evaluation, not anti-EGFR therapy.
BRAF is checked alongside RAS, but a BRAF mutation is not the prerequisite for anti-EGFR use.
Hypomagnesemia is monitored during anti-EGFR therapy but it is not the selection criterion.

questions.q: Where does prostate adenocarcinoma most often arise, and how does that differ from benign prostatic hyperplasia?
ch: Both arise in the central zone, which is why the two cannot be distinguished on examination
Cancer arises in the anterior fibromuscular stroma and is therefore never palpable at all
Cancer arises in the seminal vesicles and only secondarily invades the prostate gland
Cancer arises in the peripheral zone and is palpable on DRE; BPH arises in the transition zone and obstructs
Cancer arises in the transition zone and obstructs; BPH arises in the peripheral zone and is palpable
questions.exp: Prostate cancer favors the peripheral zone, which is why it is palpable as a firm, hard, or nodular area on digital rectal exam, whereas BPH arises in the transition zone and produces obstructive urinary symptoms.
why: The zonal difference is exactly what makes cancer palpable posteriorly and BPH obstructive.
Peripheral-zone tumors are classically palpable on digital rectal exam.
The tumor arises from prostatic glandular epithelium; seminal vesicle involvement is a feature of spread.
This reverses the two zones and therefore the clinical consequences.

questions.q: How is the Gleason score derived and reported?
ch: It is the percentage of biopsy cores involved, reported as Grade Groups 1 to 5
It is the sum of the two most common histologic patterns, 6-10, reported as Grade Groups 1-5
It is the PSA level multiplied by the clinical T-stage, reported as a risk category
It is the number of positive nodes added to the tumor diameter in centimeters
It is the single highest histologic pattern seen, reported on a scale of 1 to 5
questions.exp: The Gleason score is the sum of the two most common histologic patterns and runs from 6 to 10, reported as Grade Groups 1 to 5; Gleason 6 is the lowest reported score and equals Grade Group 1, and higher scores indicate more aggressive disease.
why: Core involvement informs risk, but the score itself is a sum of histologic patterns.
PSA and clinical stage are separate axes of risk stratification, not components of the score.
Nodes and tumor size belong to TNM staging, not to histologic grading.
It is a sum of two patterns rather than one, which is why the lowest reported score is 6.

questions.q: What is the characteristic radiographic appearance of prostate cancer bone metastases?
ch: Periosteal reaction with a sunburst pattern in the distal femur
Diffuse osteopenia throughout the skeleton without focal lesions
Expansile lucent lesions confined to the appendicular skeleton
Osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions of the axial skeleton — spine, pelvis, and ribs
Punched-out lytic lesions of the skull and the long bones
questions.exp: Metastatic prostate cancer is the classic cause of osteoblastic (sclerotic) bone lesions in the axial skeleton — spine, pelvis, and ribs — whereas most solid tumors go osteolytic; these lesions correlate with an elevated alkaline phosphatase and a positive bone scan.
why: A sunburst periosteal reaction suggests a primary bone tumor rather than prostate metastasis.
Diffuse bone loss is what androgen-deprivation therapy causes; metastases are focal and sclerotic.
Prostate metastases favor the axial skeleton and are sclerotic rather than lucent.
Lytic destruction is the pattern of most other solid tumors, not of prostate cancer.

questions.q: Which statement about PSA is correct?
ch: It is used to assign the Gleason Grade Group without performing a biopsy
It is cancer-specific, so any elevation above the reference range confirms malignancy
It is not cancer-specific — BPH, prostatitis, DRE, and ejaculation raise it, so trends matter more than a single value
It should be drawn after the digital rectal exam so that the gland is fully expressed
A normal PSA excludes the need for any further evaluation, imaging, or biopsy
questions.exp: PSA is the key serum marker for screening and monitoring, but it is not cancer-specific: BPH, prostatitis, a digital rectal exam, and ejaculation all raise it, so trends and PSA velocity matter more than one number.
why: Grade Group comes from histology on a biopsy specimen; PSA cannot supply it.
Many benign conditions raise PSA, so an elevation does not confirm cancer.
The sample is drawn before the DRE, because the examination itself can transiently raise the value.
An abnormal DRE or a rising trend still warrants MRI and biopsy despite a value in range.

questions.q: Why is a GnRH agonist such as leuprolide paired with an antiandrogen when androgen-deprivation therapy is started?
ch: To prevent the initial testosterone flare, which can worsen tumor flare and cord compression
To protect bone density and prevent osteonecrosis of the jaw during therapy
To speed the fall in testosterone so that castrate levels are reached within hours
To prevent the hypokalemia and hypertension caused by mineralocorticoid excess
To reduce the seizures and falls seen with androgen-receptor pathway inhibitors
questions.exp: GnRH agonists cause an initial testosterone flare, so they are covered with an antiandrogen such as bicalutamide to prevent tumor flare and worsening spinal cord compression; a GnRH antagonist such as degarelix or relugolix suppresses immediately without a flare when rapid control is needed.
why: Bone protection comes from denosumab or zoledronic acid with calcium and vitamin D, and osteonecrosis of the jaw is a risk of those agents.
Immediate suppression comes from switching to an antagonist, not from adding an antiandrogen to an agonist.
Mineralocorticoid excess is the abiraterone problem, managed with concurrent prednisone.
Seizures and falls are enzalutamide effects; darolutamide has fewer CNS effects.

questions.q: A man is started on abiraterone with prednisone. Which set of adverse effects should be monitored?
ch: Gynecomastia and hot flashes as the principal expected toxicities
Neutropenia requiring a complete blood count before every cycle
Seizures, falls, and fatigue from central nervous system effects
Osteonecrosis of the jaw and hypocalcemia after the first dose
Hypokalemia, hypertension, fluid retention, and liver enzyme elevation
questions.exp: Abiraterone is a CYP17 inhibitor given with prednisone; the mineralocorticoid excess it produces causes hypokalemia, hypertension, and fluid retention, and liver enzymes must be followed.
why: Gynecomastia and hot flashes are the bicalutamide profile.
Neutropenia monitoring belongs to docetaxel chemotherapy.
Those are enzalutamide effects among the androgen-receptor pathway inhibitors.
Those belong to the bone-targeted agents denosumab and zoledronic acid.

questions.q: What must be done before starting denosumab or zoledronic acid in metastatic prostate cancer?
ch: Document a castrate testosterone level and a rising PSA on two occasions
Correct hypocalcemia, give calcium and vitamin D, and obtain dental clearance
Obtain a baseline echocardiogram and then repeat it every three months
Confirm RAS wild-type status in the tumor before giving the first dose
Withhold all androgen-deprivation therapy for the duration of treatment
questions.exp: Before a bone-targeted agent, hypocalcemia is corrected and calcium and vitamin D are given, and a dental evaluation is obtained because osteonecrosis of the jaw is the feared complication.
why: That describes the definition of castration resistance, not the safety checklist for these drugs.
Serial cardiac imaging is not the prerequisite for starting a bone-targeted agent.
RAS testing belongs to anti-EGFR therapy in colorectal cancer, not to bone protection here.
Bone agents are given alongside ADT, partly to treat the bone loss that ADT causes.

questions.q: A man with metastatic prostate cancer reports new back pain with leg weakness and urinary retention. What is the priority?
ch: Schedule an outpatient bone scan within the next two weeks
Start an oral opioid and reassess the pain at the next clinic visit
Begin a GnRH agonist alone to shrink the metastatic deposits
Order a PSA and alkaline phosphatase and await the results
Emergent MRI with corticosteroids, then radiation or surgery for cord compression
questions.exp: New back pain with leg weakness, saddle anesthesia, or bladder and bowel dysfunction signals malignant spinal cord compression — a neuro-oncologic emergency requiring urgent MRI, steroids, and radiation or surgery.
why: A delayed outpatient scan misses the window in which neurologic function can be salvaged.
Analgesia alone ignores the neurologic deficit that defines this emergency.
An agonist alone risks a testosterone flare that would worsen the cord compression.
Laboratory trends cannot exclude cord compression, and waiting for them delays imaging.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man has Grade Group 1 (Gleason 6) cancer in two cores with a low PSA. Which management does the module support?
ch: Active surveillance, since many men die with prostate cancer rather than of it
Androgen-deprivation therapy plus an androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor
Docetaxel chemotherapy followed by radium-223 directed at the bone
Bilateral orchiectomy with denosumab added for bone protection
Immediate radical prostatectomy to remove all of the disease
questions.exp: Active surveillance is the recommended approach for low-risk Grade Group 1 disease, because many men die with prostate cancer rather than of it; definitive local therapy is reserved for intermediate- and high-risk disease.
why: ADT-based systemic therapy is for advanced or metastatic disease.
Docetaxel and radium-223 are used in high-volume metastatic and castration-resistant disease.
Castration plus bone-protective therapy is far beyond what low-risk localized disease requires.
Definitive local therapy is matched to intermediate- and high-risk disease, not to Grade Group 1.

questions.q: A man with metastatic prostate cancer is found to carry a germline BRCA2 mutation. What are the implications?
ch: Anti-HER2 therapy with trastuzumab becomes the treatment of choice for him
His bone metastases will now be osteolytic rather than osteoblastic in pattern
The cancer tends to be more aggressive and may respond to a PARP inhibitor such as olaparib
PSA can no longer be used to monitor his response to systemic therapy
The disease is typically indolent and is best managed by surveillance alone
questions.exp: BRCA2 carriers develop more aggressive prostate cancer and may respond to PARP inhibitors such as olaparib, which is why germline testing is recommended in high-risk or metastatic disease.
why: Trastuzumab targets HER2-amplified breast cancer and has no role here.
Prostate cancer metastases remain characteristically osteoblastic regardless of germline status.
PSA remains the marker tracked during systemic therapy.
BRCA2-associated disease is more aggressive, the opposite of an indolent surveillance candidate.

questions.q: Which description fits the majority of pancreatic cancers?
ch: Lymphoma arising in peripancreatic nodes and invading the gland secondarily
Acinar cell carcinoma of the tail, presenting with early painless jaundice
Ductal adenocarcinoma of exocrine duct epithelium, 60-70% in the head of the pancreas
Neuroendocrine tumors of the islet cells, which carry a far better prognosis
Squamous cell carcinoma arising from the main pancreatic duct epithelium
questions.exp: Most cases are pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) arising from exocrine duct epithelium, and roughly 60-70% occur in the head of the pancreas, where they obstruct the common bile duct.
why: Pancreatic cancer is a primary epithelial malignancy of the gland itself.
Tail tumors present late with vague back pain and weight loss; painless jaundice is the head-tumor presentation.
PNETs behave very differently and carry a far better prognosis, but they are only a minority of pancreatic cancers.
The duct epithelium gives rise to adenocarcinoma, not squamous carcinoma.

questions.q: An older adult has painless jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and a palpable non-tender gallbladder. What does this combination indicate?
ch: Courvoisier sign — malignant distal biliary obstruction, typically a pancreatic head cancer
A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor of the tail producing hormonal symptoms
Acute cholecystitis caused by a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck
Choledocholithiasis, in which the gallbladder is scarred and non-distensible
Viral hepatitis producing a hepatocellular pattern of hyperbilirubinemia
questions.exp: A palpable, non-tender gallbladder with jaundice is the Courvoisier sign, which points to malignant distal biliary obstruction — a pancreatic head cancer until proven otherwise.
why: A tail lesion does not obstruct the bile duct, and PNETs present with hormonal syndromes instead.
Cholecystitis produces a tender gallbladder with pain and fever, not painless jaundice.
Courvoisier's law is exactly the point: gallstone disease leaves a scarred, non-distensible gallbladder, so a distended one argues against stones.
Hepatitis gives a hepatocellular pattern without pale stools or a distended gallbladder from duct obstruction.

questions.q: Which mutation is the near-universal driver in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma?
ch: Mismatch-repair gene loss, producing microsatellite instability in most tumors
APC, lost as the first hit in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence
KRAS, activated in more than 90% of cases
BRCA2, present in the majority of sporadic tumors
HER2/ERBB2 amplification, driving growth-factor signaling
questions.exp: Activating KRAS mutations are present in more than 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma — the near-universal driver — with loss of CDKN2A, TP53, and SMAD4 completing the stepwise progression from PanIN precursor lesions.
why: Mismatch-repair deficiency defines the MSI pathway of Lynch syndrome tumors, not most PDAC.
APC loss initiates the colorectal adenoma-carcinoma sequence, not pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
BRCA2 is a hereditary risk factor in a minority of patients, not the near-universal driver.
HER2 amplification is a breast cancer driver and a therapeutic target there.

questions.q: How should CA 19-9 be used in pancreatic cancer?
ch: As a reliable value in every patient, since cholestasis does not affect it
For baseline prognosis and for monitoring response or recurrence — never for screening
As a screening test in anyone with new-onset diabetes after the age of 50
As the definitive diagnostic test, replacing tissue confirmation by EUS-FNA
As the marker that determines resectability and the choice of operation
questions.exp: CA 19-9 is used for prognosis and to monitor treatment response and recurrence, never for screening; it is falsely low in Lewis-antigen-negative patients and falsely elevated by cholestasis.
why: Cholestasis falsely elevates it, and Lewis-antigen-negative patients do not express it at all.
New-onset diabetes after age 50 with weight loss is a clinical clue that prompts imaging, but the marker is still not a screening test.
Tissue diagnosis comes from EUS with fine-needle aspiration; a tumor marker cannot replace it.
Resectability is determined by vascular involvement on pancreatic-protocol CT.

questions.q: A patient with pancreatic cancer has steatorrhea, malabsorption, and continuing weight loss. What is the appropriate treatment, and how is it taken?
ch: Celiac plexus neurolysis performed for opioid-refractory visceral pain
A scheduled high-dose opioid, with a bowel regimen to pre-empt constipation
Low-molecular-weight heparin injected daily to reduce the thrombotic risk
Pancreatic enzyme replacement (pancrelipase) with every meal and snack, beads not crushed
An endoscopic biliary stent placed at ERCP to relieve the obstruction
questions.exp: Exocrine insufficiency causing steatorrhea, malabsorption, and weight loss is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement (pancrelipase) taken with every meal and snack; the enteric-coated beads must not be crushed.
why: A neurolytic block is a pain intervention and does nothing for steatorrhea.
Opioids treat severe visceral cancer pain and would worsen, not correct, malabsorption.
LMWH addresses this cancer's high thrombogenicity, not exocrine insufficiency.
A stent relieves obstructive jaundice and pruritus; it does not replace pancreatic enzymes.

questions.q: A pancreatic head mass is suspected. What is the correct order of the workup?
ch: CA 19-9 first, proceeding to surgery only if the level is elevated
Pancreatic-protocol contrast CT first for detection and staging, then EUS-FNA for tissue
PET scan first, followed by percutaneous biopsy of the largest lesion
EUS-FNA first, with imaging only if the biopsy is non-diagnostic
ERCP with brushings first, and CT only if the brushings are negative
questions.exp: Pancreatic-protocol contrast CT is first-line for detection and staging, and EUS with fine-needle aspiration then supplies the tissue diagnosis; biopsy of a clearly resectable mass is avoided when it would delay surgery.
why: The marker is for prognosis and monitoring and cannot select patients for an operation.
Pancreatic-protocol CT, not PET, is the first-line study for detection and staging.
Staging imaging comes first, because it defines resectability and may make biopsy unnecessary before surgery.
ERCP assesses and decompresses the biliary tree and carries a pancreatitis risk; it is not the first staging step.

questions.q: Which structures does a Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) remove?
ch: The pancreatic head alone, leaving the duodenum and bile duct intact
The duodenum and gallbladder only, sparing all pancreatic tissue
The entire pancreas together with the spleen and the distal stomach
The pancreatic head, duodenum, distal bile duct, gallbladder, and part of the stomach
The pancreatic body and tail together with the spleen
questions.exp: A Whipple (pancreaticoduodenectomy) removes the pancreatic head, the duodenum, the distal bile duct, the gallbladder, and part of the stomach; distal tumors instead undergo distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy.
why: The duodenum and distal bile duct are resected along with the head.
The operation exists precisely to remove the pancreatic head tumor.
The Whipple is a head resection, not a total pancreatectomy with splenectomy.
That describes distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy, the operation for body and tail tumors.

questions.q: A man with pancreatic adenocarcinoma develops migratory superficial thrombophlebitis. What does this represent, and how is cancer-associated VTE treated?
ch: A local infection of the vein, treated with antibiotics and warm compresses
A drug reaction to gemcitabine, managed by holding the next infusion
An expected consequence of biliary stenting that needs no specific therapy
Exocrine insufficiency, treated by increasing the enzyme replacement dose
Trousseau syndrome, a paraneoplastic clue; LMWH is preferred over warfarin
questions.exp: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis is the Trousseau sign of malignancy, a classic paraneoplastic association with pancreatic adenocarcinoma and a marker of its strong hypercoagulability; low-molecular-weight heparin is preferred over warfarin for active-cancer VTE.
why: The migratory pattern marks a paraneoplastic thrombotic process, not an infection.
Gemcitabine toxicity is myelosuppression and neuropathy, not migratory thrombophlebitis.
Stent complications are pancreatitis, cholangitis, and occlusion, and this finding does need anticoagulation.
Exocrine insufficiency causes steatorrhea and weight loss, not thrombophlebitis.

questions.q: What determines whether a pancreatic adenocarcinoma is resectable, borderline resectable, locally advanced, or metastatic?
ch: The presence of painless jaundice with a palpable non-tender gallbladder
Whether the tumor arises in the head rather than in the body or the tail
The CA 19-9 level at diagnosis and its rate of change over time
The histologic grade reported on the EUS-FNA specimen
Involvement of the SMA, celiac axis, and SMV-portal confluence, plus distant spread
questions.exp: Resectability is classified surgically by vascular involvement — the superior mesenteric artery, the celiac axis, and the SMV-portal confluence — together with distant metastasis, and that classification dictates upfront surgery versus neoadjuvant therapy.
why: Courvoisier sign points to the diagnosis and its location, not to resectability.
Location determines which operation is performed, not whether resection is possible.
CA 19-9 is prognostic and used for monitoring; it does not define the resectability category.
Grade informs prognosis, but the surgical categories are anatomic and vascular.

questions.q: Three days after a biliary stent was placed at ERCP, a patient develops fever, worsening jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain. What is this?
ch: Ascending cholangitis (Charcot triad) — an emergency needing decompression and antibiotics
Post-ERCP pancreatitis, which resolves with observation and early oral intake
Expected pruritus from cholestasis, treated with cool compresses and skin care
Delayed gastric emptying, a recognized complication after a Whipple procedure
A pancreatic fistula from the anastomosis, managed with enzyme replacement
questions.exp: Fever, jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain make up the Charcot triad of ascending cholangitis after biliary obstruction or ERCP — a medical emergency requiring urgent decompression and antibiotics.
why: Post-ERCP pancreatitis is a real risk, but fever with rising bilirubin and RUQ pain points to biliary infection.
Pruritus is a symptom of cholestasis and does not explain fever and pain.
Delayed gastric emptying follows a Whipple resection, and this patient had a stent placed.
A fistula is a post-operative complication of resection, and enzyme replacement is not its treatment.
